record.paper_title: Stellar model calibrations with the Ai Phe binary system. Open questions about the robustness of the fit
record.original_question: When fitting stellar models to a precisely observed binary system such as Ai Phe, do different stellar codes, inference pipelines, or modelling assumptions about microscopic diffusion and other extra-mixing processes produce different estimates of the system age and convective core overshooting efficiency? If they do, to what extent are the inferred calibration parameters properties of the stars themselves rather than artifacts of the modeller's chosen input physics and estimation pipeline?

evidence.quote: Different stellar codes, relying on different assumptions about the microscopic diffusion efficiency, and given the inclusion of extra-mixing mechanisms, may obtain different age and/or overshooting efficiency calibrations on the same target system.
It is well known that different pipelines, adopting different estimation algorithms and different stellar tracks, might obtain different estimates of the system fundamental parameters
great care should be taken when adopting binary systems for parameter calibrations, because the obtained parameters may only reflect the decisions by the modellers in their stellar model computations

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a detached eclipsing binary system whose two stellar components have masses, radii, effective temperatures, and surface metallicities determined to high precision by photometric and spectroscopic observations. A stellar evolution pipeline takes such observational constraints as input and returns estimates of two calibration parameters: (i) the common age t of the system, and (ii) the convective core overshooting efficiency β (parametrized, e.g., as the fraction of the local pressure scale height by which the convective core boundary is extended). Such a pipeline depends on choices including the stellar evolution code, the prescription and efficiency of microscopic diffusion of heavy elements, the inclusion or omission of additional extra-mixing processes (e.g., rotational mixing, thermohaline mixing, turbulent mixing), the adopted nuclear reaction rates and opacities, the input grid of evolutionary tracks, and the statistical estimation algorithm used to match models to observations.

Formulate and answer the following questions:

(a) Given a fixed set of observational constraints for such a binary, do two different pipelines that differ only in their assumptions about microscopic diffusion efficiency and the presence of extra-mixing mechanisms generically produce statistically distinguishable estimates of (t, β)?

(b) Quantify the spread in the inferred (t, β) induced by varying (i) the stellar evolution code, (ii) the diffusion/extra-mixing prescriptions, and (iii) the estimation algorithm, while keeping the observational data fixed.

(c) Determine to what extent the resulting calibration values (t, β) reflect intrinsic properties of the binary system, as opposed to systematic artifacts of the modeller's chosen input physics and inference procedure, and identify conditions (if any) under which the inferred parameters can be regarded as code-independent properties of the stars.
artifact.status_search_result: Systematic differences among stellar evolution codes and input physics in calibrating ages and overshooting from binaries are a known, ongoing methodological issue in stellar astrophysics; no universally accepted resolution exists, and the question of code-independence of inferred calibrations remains open as of recent literature.

status_evidence.title: Stellar model calibrations with the Ai Phe binary system
status_evidence.snippet: Different stellar codes, relying on different assumptions about microscopic diffusion and extra-mixing, may obtain different age and/or overshooting calibrations on the same target.
status_evidence.claim: The systematic dependence of inferred age and overshooting on modelling choices is identified but not resolved.
